records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) field for this species is alphabetized and opens with Baby's Tears, running Baby's Tears, Flamingo Plant, Freckle Face, Measles Plant, Pink Splash, Polka Dot Plant. RHS's dedicated Hypoestes phyllostachya (v) page renders 'polka dot plant' as the plant-profile subtitle beneath its botanical name and files flamingo plant, freckle face, measles plant and pink dot under a separate Other common names field. 'Polka Dot Plant' is landed as the name RHS's dedicated single-species page leads with. RHS's trailing '(v)' marks the variegated form and is not part of the binomial, so scientific_name_accepted reads Hypoestes phyllostachya.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox tags this species "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses", and "#non-toxic for dogs". The page carries no separate Poison or Poisonous-to-Humans section, so no additional symptom, poison-part, or severity detail is available for this species.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail rely entirely on NC State's Tags block ('#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for horses', '#non-toxic for dogs'); the page has no separate Poison or Poisonous-to-Humans section, so no human-toxicity or symptom detail exists to capture.

humidity_need left null: the dedicated RHS species page does state a humidity need, but as a straddling range -- 'Grow indoors in peat-free, loam-based potting compost in bright, filtered light, with moderate to high humidity.' -- which does not resolve to a single enum token. RHS's genus-level guide is more emphatic ('Hypoestes need high humidity to keep their foliage looking good'), but that text is on the shared genus page and was excluded per scope discipline. NC State's species page lists 'Deer' and 'Humidity' under Resistance To Challenges (tolerance tags), which does not state a humidity need level.

chill_damage_f left null: the only minimum-temperature figure found -- RHS's genus-level growing guide, 'The temperature should always be at least 12°C (54°F).' -- is (a) on the shared genus page, not the dedicated species page, and (b) a comfort/keep-above minimum rather than a damage-onset temperature. The species page carries only a hardiness rating (H1B, site-wide legend '(10 - 15)') and NC State gives only USDA Zones 10a-11b, both survival/zone figures. No admissible species-specific damage-onset temperature was found.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_pct_min/max, and light_fc_min/good left null: no admissible source gave day/night temperature ranges, numeric humidity percentages, or foot-candle light figures for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only hour figure ('2-6 hours') is the site-wide light-category legend text bundled into the Partial Shade tag's parenthetical description, not species-specific prose, and is excluded per the rules.

outdoor_sun_exposure includes only part_shade. RHS's structured Position field on the dedicated species page lists 'Full sun, Partial shade,' but NC State's structured Light field for this species lists only Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade (no full sun); per the cross-source-conflict rule, the RHS-only full_sun value was left out.

soil_drainage left null: NC State gives a bare 'Good Drainage' tag and RHS gives a bare 'Well-drained' Moisture field; neither source pairs 'well-drained' with a moisture qualifier ('moist but...') or an explicit sharp/sandy, dry-tolerant, no-wet-tolerance description, so per the rules this stays ambiguous rather than 'fast.'
soil_ph_min left null: NC State's Acid band is rendered as the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)', so no floor value can be set from it.

water_regime left null: RHS's dedicated species page states only 'Water freely in growth and sparingly in winter,' which does not map cleanly onto the keep_moist/keep_barely_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between scale. RHS's genus-level growing guide says 'Keep the compost moist but allow the surface to dry out slightly between waterings' (which would suggest dry_surface_between), but that text is on the genus page, not the species page, and was excluded per scope discipline.
water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: no admissible source framed watering in those terms for this species.
fertilize_strength left null: RHS's fertilizing sentence names a 'balanced liquid fertiliser' but states no dilution/strength fraction.
fertilize_interval_days uses the upper bound (21 days) of RHS's literal 'every 2-3 weeks' cadence, since the schema takes a single number; the true stated interval is a 14-21 day range.
fertilize_active_months ([6,7,8]) is our reading of RHS's 'in summer' phrase under the UK seasonal convention (June-August); RHS did not enumerate specific calendar months on this species page.

records.cool_rest_note: RHS advises watering moderately when in active growth and sparingly in winter, indicating a drier winter rest. Neither source calls for a cooler winter -- NC State states the plant does not tolerate temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and that container plants need to be brought indoors during the winter.
records.name_note: NC State gives this species a dedicated common-name page whose H1 leads with 'Purple Heart' over the scientific name Tradescantia pallida; its species page lists Purple Heart second in an alphabetized four-item Common Name(s) list (Moses in the Basket, Purple Heart, Purple Queen, Purple Spiderwort) in the same order as that page's title parenthetical, and the common-name page omits Purple Heart from that same field because it is that page's lead name. RHS's dedicated species page renders 'purple-heart spiderwort' as the subtitle beneath its Tradescantia pallida heading. Purple Heart is used here as the form NC State's dedicated page leads with; RHS's hyphenated purple-heart spiderwort is the same name with 'spiderwort' appended. Moses in the Basket, Purple Queen and Purple Spiderwort are alias entries only.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (human-scoped, rendered under the heading 'Poisonous to Humans:'; Poison Severity: Low; Poison Toxic Principle: unknown) lists the Poison Part as Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Stems, and gives the Poison Symptoms as: "Ingestion of the plant can cause mouth and stomach irritation for humans and pets. Contact with the sap and leaves can cause redness and skin irritation in humans and pets." The page's own banner above the Description reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Separately from that ingestion-toxicity block, NC State tags this plant Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes -- its Description repeats the hazard as prose, 'The sap from the leaves and stem can also cause skin irritation in both humans and pets.' -- and its Problems field carries five stacked tags: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs. It is the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags that carry toxic_to_pets, not the human-scoped severity rating. RHS's page carries its own separate handling warning under Potentially harmful: "Skin allergen.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". The two sources do not disagree on toxicity or edibility.

NC State agrees the plant should be moved indoors once temperatures dip below 60°F when grown outdoors in a container.
records.name_note: Sources split on which name leads, and this record lands the name the dedicated pages' lead fields carry rather than the one it was researched under. RHS's dedicated species page renders 'horsehead philodendron' as the plant-profile subtitle beneath the H1 'Philodendron bipinnatifidum' and files 'fiddle-leaf philodendron, panda plant' under Other common names; tree philodendron appears nowhere on the RHS page. Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Common Name field likewise reads 'horsehead philodendron', while its Noteworthy Characteristics prose on the same page calls the species 'commonly called tree philodendron or split leaf philodendron', so that page is split against itself. NC State's Common Name(s) field is eight alphabetized, separately linked entries that include both Horsehead Philodendron and Tree Philodendron, and its Description prose opens with 'Tree philodendron'. UF/IFAS publishes the species under the synonym Philodendron selloum, on a page titled 'Selloum, Philodendron selloum'. Two dedicated pages lead with Horsehead Philodendron and only NC State's prose leads with Tree philodendron, so Horsehead Philodendron is landed and Tree Philodendron and Split Leaf Philodendron are recorded as aliases. 'Panda Plant', which both RHS and NC State list for this species, is Kalanchoe tomentosa's landed name in this same batch, and 'Heartleaf Philodendron' belongs to Philodendron hederaceum, already in this catalog as Heart Leaf Philodendron; neither is used for this record. NC State's 'Previously known as' list carries Thaumatophyllum bipinnatifidum, the name this species was researched under, so the accepted name landed here is Philodendron bipinnatifidum.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's dedicated page carries a human-scoped Poison block, rendered under the heading 'Poisonous to Humans:', with Poison Severity 'Low', Poison Symptoms "If ingested, oral irritation, pain and swelling of mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting (not horses), and difficulty swallowing. The sap can cause skin irritation.", Poison Toxic Principle 'Calcium oxalate crystals', Causes Contact Dermatitis 'Yes', and a Poison Part list carrying all eight values: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. The page's own banner above the Description reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Separately from that human-scoped block, NC State's Problems field carries five stacked tags -- Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs -- and it is the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags that carry toxic_to_pets, not the human severity rating. NC State additionally files Poisonous as one of the four values of its Plant Type field (Houseplant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub). RHS carries its own handling warning under Potentially harmful -- "Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant/allergen.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" -- but its pet line is unscoped, reading 'Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin/eye irritant/allergen' and naming no animal, so the two sources disagree in scope and only NC State names cats and dogs. No source states an edibility counterpoint.
unknowns: No admissible source states a numeric humidity percentage, light foot-candle value, or direct-sun-hours figure specific to this species — NC State's '2-6 hours' text is the generic definition text for its site-wide Partial Shade legend tag, not species-specific prose, so humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, and direct_sun_hours_max are left null.

UF/IFAS's structured Culture > Light requirement field lists only 'part shade/part sun' and 'the shade', but its separate Use and Management prose states selloum 'actually grows quite well in full sun or partial shade' — a tolerance aside excluded by NC State's structured Light field (Dappled Sunlight, Partial Shade only) and RHS's Position field (Partial shade only). full_sun and part_sun were therefore left out of outdoor_sun_exposure despite this UF/IFAS mention.

RHS's pH field ('Acid or Alkaline or Neutral') and UF/IFAS's soil tolerances (both acidic and slightly alkaline) show no pH restriction for this species, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null rather than derived from any closed band; no admissible source gave a Neutral (6.0-8.0)-style closed range to read a ceiling from in the first place.

MoBot's own structured Water field reads 'Medium' (mid-scale), conflicting with its Culture prose stating plants 'need consistent and regular moisture and are intolerant of drought.' water_regime is set to keep_moist from the Culture prose per the rule that a bare structured Water:Medium tag functions only as a disclosed counterpoint, not primary evidence.

No admissible source gives an explicit potting-mix type (e.g. aroid mix, standard potting soil) for this species beyond describing soil texture as 'high organic matter' (NC State) or 'loam' (RHS/UF-IFAS), so soil_base is left null rather than guessed as standard_potting.

RHS's Cultivation paragraph ('Grow under glass in a peat-free, loam-based potting compost...apply a balanced liquid fertilizer monthly') reads as likely genus-level boilerplate shared across Philodendron species pages on RHS, so it was not used to support soil_base, water_regime, or the fertilize fields; no other admissible source states a fertilizing interval, active months, or dilution strength, so all three fertilize fields are left null.

day_f_max and night_f_min/max are left null: MoBot's Culture text gives only daytime temperature preferences (above 70°F in summer, above 60°F in winter) and a 60°F threshold for bringing potted plants indoors; no admissible source gives an explicit nighttime figure or an upper daytime temperature limit.

chill_damage_f (60) is derived from NC State's and MoBot's matching 'bring/move indoors below 60°F' guidance rather than a source explicitly labeling 60°F as a damage-onset temperature; flagged here since neither source uses the word 'damage.'

This is a large in-ground/houseplant shrub, not a plant any admissible source frames with a day-interval or check-depth watering schedule, so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are all left null.

common_name researched as 'Tree Philodendron'; landed as 'Horsehead Philodendron', the name RHS's plant-profile subtitle and MoBot's structured Common Name field both lead with. Tree Philodendron and Split Leaf Philodendron are kept as disclosed aliases in name_note; 'Heartleaf Philodendron' (Philodendron hederaceum, already catalogued as Heart Leaf Philodendron) and 'Panda Plant' (Kalanchoe tomentosa, landed in this same batch) are excluded, and no text was taken from either of those records.

soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's structured Soil Drainage field plus its 'moist, well-drained soil high in organic matter' sentence and RHS's Moisture field ('Moist but well-drained'). UF/IFAS's Soil tolerances list ('occasionally wet; slightly alkaline; clay; sand; acidic; loam') is retained only as a disclosed counterpoint, as is the same page's Use and Management sentence 'Although appearing as if it would need deep shade, selloum actually grows quite well in full sun or partial shade and needs fairly rich, moisture-retentive soil to look its best.' -- a wetness-tolerance list and a moisture-retentive reading that lean wetter than moderate, neither of which is a drainage field.

records.cool_rest_note: Both admissible sources call for reduced winter watering rather than a stated temperature change: NC State says tepid water should be used and watering reduced in the winter, and RHS says to water sparingly in winter after watering freely in the growing season. Neither source states a cool winter temperature, so no temperature claim is made here.
records.name_note: NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list for this species includes 'Stonecrop' alongside Burro's Tail, Donkey's Tail, Horse's Tail and Lamb's Tail, but 'Stonecrop' is a shared multi-species alias: NC State's Sedum ternatum common-name page renders a module headed 'Other plants called Stonecrop:' that lists Hylotelephium spectabile -- the accepted name of Sedum spectabile, already cataloged here as Showy Stonecrop -- alongside Sedum morganianum itself; Sedum ternatum is separately cataloged here as Three-leaved Stonecrop. RHS's dedicated single-species page leads with 'burro's tail' and its Other common names field (donkey tail, donkey's tail, horse's tail, lamb's tail) omits Stonecrop entirely. Both admissible sources therefore point to Burro's Tail, which also avoids colliding with the existing Stonecrop entries.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox tags this species non-toxic for the pet species it names, listing '#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for horses', and '#non-toxic for dogs' as separate co-listed tags. Its Edibility field states the full condition rather than an unqualified verdict: 'Stems and leaves can be eaten, but when ingested in large quantities, can cause stomach upset.' The same page also carries a handling warning relevant to physical (not chemical) risk: the leaves 'are quite delicate, do not tolerate heavy foot traffic, and will break off if manipulated.' No admissible source provided a structured Poison block (Poison Symptoms/Toxic Principle) for this species.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Cordyline fruticosa page states "This plant is toxic to dogs, cats, and horses." Its structured Problems field lists six stacked tags: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. Under the separate, human-scoped "Poisonous to Humans" heading, Poison Severity is "Low", Poison Symptoms are "Vomiting (occasionally with blood), diarrhea, lethargy, depression, anorexia, hypersalivation, dilated pupils (cats); Skin irritation or rash can occur with contact of the plant's sap.", Poison Toxic Principle is "Saponins", Causes Contact Dermatitis is "Yes", and Poison Part is "Sap/Juice" (the block's only value). The page's own banner above the Description states "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." The same paragraph carries two safety instructions: "Supervise children and pets in the presence of this plant." and "Wear gloves when handling the plant due to the risk of skin irritation." In prose, NC State separately states the human severity: "The Ti plant is considered to have a low toxicity in humans and can cause gastro-intestinal discomfort, if ingested." The Problem-for-Cats and Problem-for-Dogs tags are distinct from this human-scoped Poison block; toxic_to_pets is set true because both cats and dogs are separately named (in the "toxic to dogs, cats, and horses" sentence and again in the separate tags), not because of the human severity rating. Sources disagree on edibility: Missouri Botanical Garden's Noteworthy Characteristics for the same species says "Leaves of this plant have been used in Hawaii to make hula skirts and edible rhizomes for food.", which is disclosed here alongside NC State's toxicity framing.
